body:
How an electricity grid works

An electricity grid is an interconnected system that carries electricity from generating sources to consumers. Electricity may be generated at thermal power stations, hydroelectric plants, solar installations, wind farms and other facilities. It travels through transmission and distribution networks before reaching homes, farms, commercial establishments and industries.

Large generating stations generally supply electricity to the transmission network. Transmission lines carry bulk electricity over relatively long distances, while distribution networks deliver electricity to consumers. Smaller generating sources, such as rooftop solar installations, may connect directly to the distribution network.

Why continuous balancing is necessary

The defining operational requirement of an electricity grid is that electricity supply and demand must remain balanced continuously. The amount of electricity entering the system must be matched by consumption and network losses, while accounting for electricity entering or leaving storage systems.

Electricity cannot simply accumulate in transmission lines for later use. If available generation is insufficient for the load, the system must obtain additional electricity, release stored energy or reduce demand. If generation exceeds what the system can absorb, it must reduce some generation, increase suitable consumption, charge storage or transfer electricity elsewhere.

An imbalance affects the operating condition of the grid. In an interconnected alternating-current system, a shortage of generation relative to demand tends to reduce system frequency, while an excess tends to increase it. Grid operators therefore coordinate generating stations, electricity transfers and other balancing resources to maintain reliable operation.

Power and energy are different quantities

Power describes the rate at which electricity is generated or consumed at a particular moment. It is commonly measured in kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW). Energy describes the amount generated or consumed over a period and is commonly measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) or megawatt-hours (MWh).

For example, an appliance drawing 1 kW continuously for 2 hours consumes 2 kWh of electricity. A generating plant's installed capacity is therefore not the same as the energy it actually generates during a day. Actual generation depends on its operating conditions and availability.

What makes a grid smart?

A smart grid is an electricity network that uses digital measurement, communication, monitoring and control to improve the management of electricity generation, delivery and consumption.

Conventional electricity networks already require monitoring and control. A smart grid extends these capabilities by collecting more timely information from different parts of the system and enabling better coordinated responses. For example, information about household consumption, local generation and network conditions can help a utility identify changing demand and plan its response.

A smart grid does not mean that electricity itself becomes digital. Electricity continues to flow through physical conductors. The improvement lies in the information and control systems used to manage that flow.

Why renewable energy increases the importance of flexibility

Electricity demand changes throughout the day. Homes may use more electricity in the evening, while agricultural and industrial loads follow their own operating schedules. Solar and wind generation also change, but for different reasons: their output depends on available sunlight and wind.

When these variations occur together, the grid needs flexibility: the ability to adjust generation, consumption, storage or electricity transfers as conditions change. Smart meters, forecasting, demand response, transmission connections and storage can each contribute to this objective.

Prelims focus

  • Transmission carries bulk electricity; distribution delivers it to consumers.
  • Grid operation requires continuous balancing of electricity supply and demand.
  • kW and MW measure power; kWh and MWh measure energy.
  • A smart grid uses digital information and control to improve electricity-system operation.
  • Solar and wind variability creates additional needs for grid flexibility.
  • Trap: A smart grid is not a separate type of electricity-generation technology.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, chapter 'Electricity', printed pp. 199–206, and chapter 'Sources of Energy', printed pp. 242–250; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, chapter 'Infrastructure', printed pp. 144–147; International Energy Agency, Electricity 2026, section 'Flexibility', consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
What does an electricity meter measure?

An electricity meter records the electrical energy used by a consumer. The recorded consumption, generally expressed in kilowatt-hours (kWh), provides the basis for electricity billing under the applicable tariff.

A traditional electromechanical meter or a basic electronic meter can measure consumption without having a communication connection to the electricity utility. A smart meter adds communication and data-handling capabilities to electronic electricity measurement.

A smart electricity meter is an electronic meter capable of recording consumption information and supporting two-way communication with the utility through an associated metering system, usually without requiring a person to visit the premises for every reading.

Traditional meters and smart meters

FeatureTraditional or basic meterSmart meter
Energy measurementRecords electricity consumption.Records electricity consumption electronically.
Reading collectionOften requires a site visit.Supports remote collection through communication systems.
Consumption informationUsually provides a cumulative reading.Can provide readings for shorter time intervals.
Utility communicationUsually absent.Supports communication with the utility system.

A smart meter's exact capabilities depend on the meter, its communication infrastructure, the utility's systems and the services enabled. Not every smart meter automatically controls household appliances or offers every possible smart-grid feature.

Advanced Metering Infrastructure

Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) is the broader arrangement that connects smart meters with communication networks and utility data-management systems. A smart meter is one component of AMI, not the entire infrastructure.

Meter readings can travel from the consumer's premises through a communication network to the distribution utility. Information can also travel in the opposite direction, including authorised control instructions where supported. This is called two-way communication.

Two-way communication must not be confused with two-way electricity flow. Communication concerns the exchange of data. Two-way electricity flow may occur when a consumer with a permitted grid-connected rooftop solar system both imports electricity and exports surplus electricity.

How smart meters help consumers and utilities

More timely consumption information

Smart meters can provide interval-wise information rather than only an occasional cumulative reading. This helps consumers understand when electricity is being used and helps utilities study patterns of demand. It may also reduce the need for estimated meter readings.

Remote metering and system monitoring

Automated reading reduces manual collection work and can support more accurate billing and energy accounting. Depending on the installed system, smart-meter information may also assist in identifying unusual consumption patterns, communication problems and certain outage conditions.

Time-based pricing and demand management

Smart meters can support tariffs in which electricity prices differ by time period. Such arrangements may encourage consumers to use flexible appliances when electricity is more readily available or when the applicable price is lower.

However, a time-based tariff is a pricing arrangement. An actual change in electricity use in response to that price or another grid signal is a separate action called demand response.

Smart meter does not mean prepaid meter

Prepaid and postpaid describe how payment is collected. With prepaid service, the consumer pays in advance and uses the credited balance according to the applicable rules. With postpaid service, the consumer pays after electricity has been supplied and billed.

Smart-meter technology can support either arrangement. In India, prepaid smart metering has been promoted under the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), launched in July 2021. The scheme includes smart metering of consumers, distribution transformers and feeders, along with other distribution-sector improvements.

Data security and consumer information

Because smart meters communicate electricity-use information, secure communications and appropriate handling of consumer data are important. Incorrect or unauthorised access to metering information can affect privacy and trust. These concerns do not change the basic purpose of a meter: measuring electricity consumption.

Prelims focus

  • A smart meter measures electricity consumption and supports digital communication.
  • AMI includes smart meters, communication systems and utility data-management systems.
  • Two-way communication means exchange of information, not necessarily two-way electricity flow.
  • Smart metering can support interval readings, remote collection and time-based tariffs.
  • RDSS was launched in July 2021 and includes smart-meter deployment.
  • Trap: A smart meter is not necessarily prepaid, and installing one does not by itself guarantee demand response.

[Sources: Ministry of Power, Government of India, Press Information Bureau, 'Nationwide Push for Smart Prepaid Meters to Boost Distribution Efficiency and Better Consumer Services', 11 December 2025, sections on consumer benefits and utility data; Press Information Bureau, 'Progress on Smart Meter Installation under RDSS', 2 February 2026, introductory and smart-metering sections; Press Information Bureau, statement on two-way communication and load forecasting in smart metering, December 2023; consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A smart meter forms part of a communication system linking consumers and electricity utilities.

title: Smart Meters and Two-Way Information in Electricity Networks

body:
Centralised and distributed electricity generation

In a conventional centralised arrangement, electricity is produced at a relatively large generating station and delivered to consumers through the transmission and distribution networks. The generating station may be far from the places where the electricity is consumed.

Distributed generation means producing electricity at smaller generating facilities located near consumers or connected to the distribution system. Rooftop solar photovoltaic installations are a familiar example. Other examples include small local generators and certain community-scale renewable-energy installations.

Distributed generation does not automatically mean renewable generation. A local generator using conventional fuel is also a form of distributed generation. Likewise, a large solar power park connected to the bulk transmission network is generally treated as utility-scale generation rather than rooftop distributed generation.

Distributed Energy Resources

The wider term Distributed Energy Resources (DER) includes local energy resources that can contribute to electricity-system operation. These may include distributed generators, batteries and controllable electricity-consuming equipment.

This creates an important distinction: a battery is a distributed energy resource, but it is not a primary source of electricity generation. It stores energy supplied earlier and releases part of that energy when needed.

Grid-connected rooftop solar

A grid-connected rooftop solar system can supply electricity to a building while sunlight is available. If its output exceeds the building's consumption, surplus electricity may be exported to the distribution network where the connection and applicable arrangements permit it. When rooftop output is insufficient, the building may obtain the remaining electricity from the grid.

The arrangement for measuring or accounting for imported and exported electricity depends on the applicable metering and regulatory system. A solar installation should not be assumed to provide unrestricted export or automatic backup merely because it is connected to the grid.

What is a microgrid?

A microgrid is a group of interconnected electricity loads and local energy resources within defined electrical boundaries that can be controlled as one system. A suitably equipped microgrid can operate while connected to the main grid and can also operate independently when disconnected from it.

The independent operating condition is called islanded operation or islanding. When connected to the main grid, a microgrid may receive electricity from it or supply electricity to it under the permitted arrangements. During islanded operation, the microgrid must balance its local generation, storage and consumption without relying on the external grid connection.

Example: A community health facility

Consider a rural health facility equipped with rooftop solar panels, a battery and equipment that can manage local electricity supply. During normal operation, it may use rooftop electricity and obtain additional electricity from the main grid. During a grid outage, a properly configured microgrid may disconnect and continue supplying essential lighting and medical equipment.

Such backup is possible only if sufficient local electricity or stored energy is available and the system has the necessary operating and isolation capabilities. The example does not mean that a solar installation can always supply every load during an outage.

Microgrids are not the same as ordinary rooftop solar

A building may have rooftop solar panels without having a microgrid. Many ordinary grid-connected solar systems are designed to stop supplying the connected network when the utility supply fails. This prevents unintended energisation of a disconnected network.

A microgrid requires appropriate coordination and the capability to operate as a controlled local system. Solar panels, storage and local loads can be its components, but the mere presence of those components does not establish that islanded operation is possible.

Microgrids also need not use solar power. Different combinations of local generators, storage and controllable demand can be used according to the available resources and the required electricity supply.

Why distributed generation and microgrids matter

Local generation can supply some electricity close to where it is consumed. Microgrids can improve the ability of selected facilities or communities to continue operating during interruptions in the main network. They can also help organise local renewable generation and consumption.

However, distributed generation does not remove the need for the wider grid. Many consumers still need electricity from other sources at night, during unfavourable weather or when local generation and storage are insufficient.

Prelims focus

  • Distributed generation produces electricity at smaller facilities near consumers or the distribution network.
  • Rooftop solar is an example of distributed renewable generation.
  • Distributed energy resources can include generation, batteries and controllable loads.
  • A microgrid acts as a controllable local electricity system.
  • Islanding means operating independently of the main grid.
  • Trap: Rooftop solar alone does not necessarily provide islanded operation or power during a grid outage.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, chapter 'Sources of Energy', printed pp. 249–251; United States Department of Energy, 'Solar Integration: Distributed Energy Resources and Microgrids Basics', sections on distributed resources and microgrids; United States Department of Energy, 'Microgrid Systems', section defining microgrid characteristics; United States Department of Energy, 'Islanding a Microgrid', 15 October 2021; consulted 16 November 2026.]
